utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. Can I mention that because I have to deal with a second matter tomorrow, it has been necessary for us to sit tomorrow morning at 9.00 rather than in the afternoon, and we will be sitting, I believe, in this courtroom at 9.00 tomorrow morning. I hope you all enjoy the public holiday tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good morning to you too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: May I remind you that the affirmation you made to tell the truth at the beginning still applies to your evidence today. Now, Mr. Djordjevic is to continue his questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir. Good morning, Mr. Kelmendi. We will take up from where we left off yesterday.

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kelmendi, I will not ask for Exhibit P00772 to be called up again. We all remember the photograph we saw yesterday and the discussions we had about Mr. Salipur aka Munja. We were discussing the matter where you were an eyewitness of an event where he beat up an Albanian simply because he was an Albanian, and he was an innocent man. I asked you yesterday if you recalled the name of the Albanian -- Albanian who was an innocent, and I asked you whether you knew why this beating came about since you said that the man was innocent. That was my question, if I remember well.

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If you want to know the name, he is Tuf Tafilaj from Katundi i Ri. This happened about two years before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You say that you were an eyewitness of the beating up, and can you tell us why it happened and at what time?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only because he had a look at it and he was an Albanian and that bothered him that he was an Albanian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: How did you come to learn of this incident? Did you see it yourself or did you hear it from Mr. Tafilja himself?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw it with my own eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Did you subsequently give first aid to Mr. Tafilja? Did you speak to him afterwards?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was impossible to help somebody before the war and during the war because you know what kinds of rights Albanians had at that time, no rights at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Since you were an eyewitness of this incident, did you report it to the police?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't report it to the police, because I personally couldn't help anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did Mr. Tafilaj -- was he held accountable for something subsequently? Is he still alive today?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tafilaj is alive. He's a mechanic in Peja. He works as a mechanic in the Opel factory, car shop.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kelmendi, in answer to my question about the high walls surrounding houses, you said that they existed as long as there was Communism. When Communism collapsed in Kosovo, you said that you tore the walls down, and prior to that you returned your Communist Party membership cards. Were you yourself personally a member of the Yugoslav Communist Party?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't a member of that party because that was a fake party.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I asked you this because you said that you had returned membership cards, and I thought that you were among the members. Can you tell us, why did the Albanians have their houses surrounded by high walls in the Communist era? We all know that there were high walls around Albanian estates, particularly in the countryside.

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because we did not have any kind of protection from the Serbian police. We were all the time in danger, and that's why we built up the walls in order to be able to enjoy our lives.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kelmendi, I noticed that you spent a great deal of time abroad and that you were in Kosovo for some 13 years according to the statement you gave to the OTP. Will you agree with me that the police that you term Serb police also comprised Albanians?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true, but there were policemen. However, the Albanian policemen were servants to the Serbian police, that's all. We didn't have any rights.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Since you returned there in 1988 when the situation in Kosovo became more difficult - that's how you put it in your OTP statement - did you, upon your return, ever come to know that the Serb police had formed police detachments or task force comprising local people, villagers of the area? Did you have any personal knowledge of this?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question, please? I don't understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Shortly before the war, were special detachments set up comprising Albanian policemen in charge of Albanian villages, operating solely in Albanian villages? Did you know this, that the policemen of that particular detachment was Albanian, not Serbian?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a very confused question. I don't know how to answer it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Let me try and simplify my question. In your village of Cuska, were there ethnic Albanian policemen charged with maintaining law and order in Cuska?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Tell me, do you know who Karakushi is? I'm asking you about the year 1989. You said that you returned in 1988?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know this person.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't think you know him, but I suppose you will agree with me that Mr. Karakushi, an ethnic Albanian, was a police minister in 1989. I don't think it's possible that you didn't know this if you returned there in 1988.

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't want to have anything to do with people who cooperated with the Serbs, because personally, they destroyed my life.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not putting it to you that you cooperated. I only asked you if you knew that Karakushi was the police minister in 1989. Did you know that or not?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us, Mr. Kelmendi, when did you come to know of the existence of the so-called Kosovo Liberation Army, the KLA or the UCK?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: As an Albanian from Kosova, when things exacerbated we were attacked in our own homes, and I heard about the KLA. The whole world heard about them, because we were attacked. Our people were killed and our children were killed and burned. How can you attack someone in his own home where he has lived for generations, for centuries?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I understand, Mr. Kelmendi, that you are embittered by it all, but please listen to my question. My question was: When did you learn of the existence of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: When war started, and the whole world knew as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Did you know of the existence of the KLA before the war, that such units were formed?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In what way did you learn of the existence of the KLA, from whom? And I'm asking about you personally.

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the war started and civilians were being killed, I saw soldiers of the KLA, but I did not have any contact with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kelmendi, tell me, was there activity of the KLA in your village or in the -- its immediate vicinity? Mr. Kelmendi, tell me, were there members of the KLA in your village or in its immediate vicinity that you knew of?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only Agim Ceku, who was a commander. There were no other people that I know of.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How far is the village of Lodja from your village of Cuska?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Qyshk and Lodja are separated by Bistrica. Bistrica runs through them. It's about three or four kilometres as the crow flies.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Is there optical visibility between the two villages?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because Bistrica is in the middle.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Is my understanding correct, is Bistrica a river or a mountain?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a river, and there are mountains on both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In view of the proximity of that village, did you know that back in 1989 there were members of the KLA present in that village and that there was heavy fighting in the village of Lodja between Serbian forces and the KLA, in particular, in the months of July and August of 1998? Do you have any knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only know about one case. There were two hours of fighting that we could hear, but I don't know whether there were KLA members there or not. They fought there for two hours. We could hear the fighting, but maybe the KLA left the front after that, withdrew.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you said that the distance between Pec and the centre of your village is only three kilometres. You also told us that Cuska was, in actual fact, the -- in the outskirts of Pec. Did you know that Serbian policemen and soldiers and civilians were killed in Pec? Specifically, let me ask you about 1999.

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not true that Serb civilians were killed. I don't know about soldiers. I know that Salipur was killed because he -- he was a person who killed Albanians. He wanted Albanians exterminated.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know when Salipur was killed?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kelmendi, tell me, how familiar are you with the town of Pec?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: One hundred per cent, because I was born and bred there. I'm 55 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kelmendi, do you know the location of the Slavica cafe?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Slavica cafe is in Vitomirica.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You know where it is.

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in that particular cafe, on the 5th of March, 1999, the following policemen were seriously wounded -- or, rather, let me not name them, but three policemen were seriously wounded in that cafe from automatic weapons, and that was in early March of 1999.

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not true at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: What is true then?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, but it was impossible for policemen to be wounded and injured by Albanians. That's what I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that in addition to the Serbian security forces and civilians, KLA members attacked, killed, and tortured Albanian civilians as well? Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not true at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: On the 9th of March, 1999, armed members of the KLA barged into the house of the Gashi family in Pec and raped Eva Gashi. Were you aware of that? Will you agree with me that this is what happened?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is something that it's even shameful to mention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Behar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Yes. I apologise for the interruption, Your Honour, but I see that in this line of questioning we've had repeated questions now about things that appear to be well beyond the knowledge of -- of this witness, and I question whether it's relevant or appropriate to pursue questions that he's simply not familiar with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We understand the weight of what you're saying, Mr. Behar, but I think the technicality is that Mr. Djordjevic is dealing with the extent of this witness's knowledge of events of which his general evidence is to deny any knowledge. So please continue, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kelmendi, the 2nd of January, 1999, the village of Kokaj. Do you know its whereabouts? Do you know where it is?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no Kokaj in Dukagjin.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear that on the date I mentioned the KLA killed Veton Kelmendi, firing from automatic weapons? Do you know him? He is your name sake.

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kelmendi, can you tell us if you saw members of the KLA during the war and, if so, did they wear uniforms?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally did not see them, and I was not a member of the KLA. I would have liked to have been a member of the KLA, but I did not have the possibility to become a member. I never saw them. I did not have any contact with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gashi -- I'm sorry. Mr. Kelmendi. I made a mistake. Yesterday, responding to the questions of my learned friend Mr. Behar, and in the statement you made on the 22nd of May, 1998, you said from that ditch where you were hidden you saw what was going on and you tried to call the KLA to help by telephone. And now you tell us that you never saw anyone from the KLA, that you don't know anyone from the KLA, and that you don't even know what they looked like, but you did hear of them. Who were you actually calling if you never saw anyone from the KLA and never heard? You said you tried to make this phone call, but the connection was down. How come that now you don't know anyone? Can you please explain this? I would like to hear that.

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I searched all over the village of Qyshk to find someone who had connections with the KLA, because I know that after the massacre 1.240 inhabitants had -- in the same situation to face. So I tried to contact the KLA, but I failed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kelmendi, do you know who Mr. Agim Ceku is?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Ceku, a military superior army officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't think that I received a correct translation. I'm going to look at it again. Can you please give us another -- can you repeat your answer? Do you know who Agim Ceku is, because I see that you did not -- your answer is not recorded in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Again in the transcript it's not there because he's the son of Hasan Ceku. I don't know why that is like that. I would like the court to intervene so that the interpreters interpret everything that they hear. I am paying attention to this now since I know Albanian a little bit myself. I would like to ask the Albanian interpreters to translate exactly what the witness is saying.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note perhaps because of the overlap that is what is happening. It's a technical matter, not a matter of interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That is just what I was about to say, Mr. Djordjevic. There is a quick exchange between yourself and the witness, and often because another person is speaking it's impossible for the interpretation. So if you slow down, there will be what you want on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, evidently it's impossible to marry effectiveness and time efficiency and also get all the data that we're interested in, but I am going to try again.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kelmendi, would you kindly tell us who Agim Ceku is? Could you repeat your question [as interpreted] again because evidently the interpreter did not hear what you said.

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Agim Ceku is the son of Hasan Ceku, a superior army officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Hasan Ceku was killed. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Agim Ceku was a high-ranking officer of the KLA, a commander. Do you agree with me that that's how it was?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kelmendi, in view of your testimony from yesterday and what is contained in your statement, you said that you tried to reach somebody from the KLA by telephone. This is how you responded to the question from the Prosecutor, and that was also what you said in your statement to the investigator on the 20th of May, 2008. I am asking you -- I understand why you called, but I'm asking you, Who did you call?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have any chance to call anyone because the connection was down. So I was unable to contact anyone. My concern was to have someone accompany the civilian population, because I was afraid for their fate.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We understood that as well, sir, that you didn't reach anyone because the connection was down, but what I'm asking you is who were you calling? Who was it that you wanted to call?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have in mind any particular name. I was simply interested in finding someone, just anyone, because I wanted to be able to assist the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Again I say I understand you completely, but I'm asking you again, who was it that you were calling in order to get to the KLA through that person? This is what you said. This is why I'm asking you this question.

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wanted to find someone to contact, but I couldn't because I didn't have any particular name or last name in mind. Nevertheless, I tried. I simply attempted to find someone in the KLA, but I didn't have in mind any particular person, that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You did call someone. Who was it who knew about KLA contacts that you needed to help you? Who did you call? You said this yourself, so we need to clarify this. You are responding to my questions by saying something that everyone knows. All I'm asking you is to say who was it that you called in your attempts to reach the KLA.

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even in my statement that I gave, and today I am repeating that I didn't call anyone. I did not have a chance, because I didn't have any connections to anyone in the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let's leave it at that, but I don't understand, then, what you were trying to say when you said that in your statement. You said that you were trying to find somebody all day from the KLA in the village. This would imply that you were moving around during the events of the 14th of May of 1999, looking for somebody from the KLA in the village who would be able to help and protect the civilians. Can you please tell me where these policemen were when you were able to move around freely and look for someone to -- from the KLA to protect the civilians? Can you please tell us a little bit about that.

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the massacre in Qyshk, they went to Pavlan, and they did the same thing there, from Pavlan to Zahaq. It was the same group. About 80 persons were executed and their bodies burned.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me -- well, let's go back to the events from Pec. Do you know that in a cafe in Pec seven Serb young men were killed from automatic weapons in the course of one evening? Do you know this? I'm talking about civilians.

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: At what time did that happen?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: It happened -- I don't know exactly, whether it was in 1998 or 1999, but I know that it did happen. Would you agree with me that it is how it was? It would be strange if you didn't know anything about it in view of the fact that you practically lived in Pec.

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not true at all. It is impossible for Albanians to kill Serb civilians, because Albanians have a great heart, and they wanted and they did protect the Serbians like their brothers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So you don't have any information about this event.

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not true what you are saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kelmendi, in paragraph 8 of your statement of the 22nd of May, 2008, you said that you saw how the police and the army were surrounding your village. Can you please tell me how you saw this attempt to surround the village. And after you came from the fields, can you please tell us the direction that the police and the army or the police or the army were deploying around your village? Since you were an eyewitness of this incident, did the police go to one place, the military to another? Were they mixed up? Can you please explain this and give us some details about it?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the morning of the 14th of May, 1999, I took my cattle out at 4.00 in the morning. You had to do that early, before it became light, because during light, during the day time, the situation was not very secure. It was dangerous. So I took my cattle to the meadow, to pasture. When it became 6.00, I saw the police and the army in lines, in formations, surrounding the village. They started at Met Shala [phoen] -- Shala whom they killed and then they killed Ali Berisha.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Were you able to clarify -- to differentiate clearly between the police and the army or not? But if you were, how was it that you were able to differentiate between them?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could differentiate from their clothes and the persons. I knew that there were more police forces than army forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: So they were not all dressed the same.

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Please describe to us the kind of uniforms that you saw. Can you describe to us what kind of uniforms they wore?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police were dressed in blue camouflage uniform. The army, green camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Did they have any kind of insignia on the uniforms? Did you notice anything like that?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police who patrolled the asphalt, they had insignia. Those who entered the village, the village resembled the Ninjas you see in the movies. Their faces were all painted up. It was impossible for you to tell who was who. Only you could see the whites of their eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 11 of your statement you describe these 80-odd persons, as you said. You said that they were wearing camouflage colours, T-shirts and trousers, prevailing green or blue. When you say that, were they all masked? You said that their faces had camouflage on them. Did they look neat, like regular soldiers, or did they have long hair or scarves? Did they all look different? These are several questions. If you're able to answer them, okay. If not, I will put the questions one by one, but any way, you can try.

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That day when the forces came, the Serb forces came to the village. They had T-shirts with short sleeves. That's a fact. And they were masked. They were between 35 to 50 years of age. They didn't have long hair. They were regular people. None of them had a beard.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Did they have caps -- caps on their heads or anything like a ribbon on their forehead or something?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had a black bandanna, some of them, but they didn't have caps. They had only black scarves tied round their heads.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't get an answer about the uniforms that they were wearing, either the green or the blue camouflage ones, if you noticed any kind of insignia or markings on the uniforms.

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only -- you could tell from the colour of the trousers only who was a soldier, who was police, because on the upper part of their bodies they were wearing T-shirts with short sleeves.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How did you conclude -- you said that today, and you said that in your statement in paragraph 13, you said that those people were between 35 and 50 years old, and you said that they were wearing camouflage on their faces. How were you able to tell what age they were?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could tell from the way they moved about that they were between 35 and 50. They were very agile in their movements.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you are describing the soldiers, and you said that they were carrying Kalashnikovs produced in Yugoslavia, that they had shells, and they also had these large long knives tucked in their belts. Did they all have these knives? Can you describe them? Were these military-issue knives like bayonets which are issued with rifles, or were these knives that looked completely different, but you said that they were large and long.

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They were special knives to kill Albanian civilians. You cannot kill someone through a bayonet. They were special knives to kill innocent civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: They were all wearing them?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some, yes; some, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: More of them or fewer?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were more wearing knives and less not wearing them. Two-thirds had knives. One-third did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: When they finally entered the village, you were behind the house of Deme Gashi, in that ditch that was covered by vegetation, and you had good -- you had a good overview of what was going on from Deme Gashi's house. Can you tell me, at that point in time where was the police in the village?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The place the massacre took place I would say was in the centre of the village. They came from Peja, and they met at the graveyard of the heroes. They came from three different directions, from the asphalt road, from one part of the village, and from Bistrice, and they rallied the population in the middle of the village near the cemetery, and then they, as you know, committed the massacre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: The place where you were hiding at that point in time, how far was it from the place where the policemen were? From the centre of the village.

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approximately 80 metres I was away from that place where they separated the men from the women and the children. Maybe less than 80 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, behind you and behind Deme Gashi's house, what is there?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Various ditch, and then there is a mountain.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Behind you. Behind the place where you were lying at that point.

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Were there any members of the Serb security forces there at the time?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is interesting to know that when there was a mountain behind them, when they didn't feel secure behind their backs, they didn't go. They were brave only with the civilians, whom they massacred.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell me, in paragraph 21 you described the kind of weapons that the members of the Serbian forces had, and you said how the barrels looked. This is in paragraph 21. We have that information, so I'm not going to ask you about that, but in paragraph 23 you say that the army was using a different kind of weapon from the one used by the police. I think that it would be good for you to explain to all of us what you meant by that, and can you please explain the difference between the weapons used by the police and the weapons used by the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The army had the weapons with the wooden butt, whereas the police had the weapons with the metallic butt. They had snipers with dum dum bullets.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Are you sure when you say that, that this was the case in 100 per cent of the cases and that they didn't have the collapsible -- the Kalashnikovs with the collapsible metal rifle butts?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not 100 per cent but 1.000 per cent is true what I'm saying, because I eyewitnessed everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kelmendi, based on what we heard during the examination-in-chief, I understood that all these people were armed with Yugoslav manufactured Kalashnikovs from the Kraguje -- Crvena Zastava factory but with a collapsible butt, not a wooden butt. Am I correct when I say that?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You say that there were people in military camouflage uniforms and now you described them as members of the military, but they don't have rifles with wooden butts. Were there any other weapons other than Kalashnikovs? When I ask about that, I'm thinking about firearms.

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they had machine-guns. Machine-guns they had. The ones that are worn by the infantry troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And the jeep that you described, what sort of weapons were on the jeep? What sort of a machine-gun was mounted on it? You mentioned that.

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... make. The others had submachine-guns. It was a Gulinov make.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: It seems that I'm going too fast again and that we're having some problems with the interpretation, but all right. What colour was the jeep?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is known what the colour of the jeeps -- the army colour. It was green, and it did not have a roof.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Let's move on to paragraph 24 and 25, as well as paragraph 27, where you refer to Klicina or Klincina, and you say that Obrnovic was the commander of the police station of Klicina or Klincina. Can you tell us the right name of the location?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Klicina with a K, Klicina.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What's the distance between that village and yours?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 5 or 6 kilometres. I never measured the distance, but I think that's about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you explain to us why was it that the policemen there Klicina should come to the outskirts of Pec, this is to say to your village, and conduct certain investigation activities? Didn't -- didn't your village have a police force, or close to your village?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because at Zastava there was a police check-point. They had set up a police check-point there. It was between Peja and Qyshk. And the Klicina police and Obrnovic -- I knew him because he was from Klicina. The asphalt road was guarded by the policemen from Klicina.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that the reason why you talked to Obrnovic from Klicina was solely the fact that you knew the man and nothing else? The conversation was not of an official nature. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke to him before the war. During the war I never spoke to him. I kept a distance, because I knew what my fate would be if I met him. It was either die or escape to live.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Did you personally have any sort of trouble with Obrnovic?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have problems with Obrnovic but with somebody else, because someone was trying to kill me and injured my eye and my jaw, but God willed that I lived, because they really wanted to kill me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Who and when?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Rank Vlahovic, before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, was Obrnovic hostile towards you? And I mean the Obrnovic from Klicina.

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is surprising, because all the policemen that were there had this hatred in them against us, this great hatred for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Including Obrnovic?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of them were the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You say in paragraph 27 of your statement that Obrnovic sent Mijo Brajovic -- first of all, did you know Mijo Brajovic before the war?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mijo Brajovic is from Zahaq. He -- he used to be a combine driver, and he used to harvest for the Albanians in the past, and I knew him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You said that Obrnovic sent Mijo Brajovic off to check whether the villagers were armed and whether there were any members of the KLA there on the 14th of -- on the 13th of May. First of all, how did you know that Mijo Brajovic was dispatched there by Obrnovic and not by somebody else?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because on the 13th when Mijo came to my house, because that's where he came, I gave him a cigarette that he lit. He called me Jaran, and he said: "Jaran, don't worry. There will be police coming. They will come to ask you whether you have guns, and nothing will happen to you." But their purpose, their real purpose was for us to remain there and for them to do what they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, how did you come to know that Brajovic was sent by Obrnovic? That's my question for you.

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course he had sent him. Who else could have sent him? He wanted to get information. He was not inviting us to a wedding. He just wanted to see what the situation was like in the village and to prepare the village for the massacre the next day. They had plans. They had programmes to commit what they did it -- what they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, this is a conclusion of yours. You don't have any other information. This is my question: On the following day, the 14th of May, 1999, did you see Obrnovic and Brajovic in the village?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on the asphalt road. They were patrolling there. And from their car, Avdi Banushi was killed right in front of my eyes. I saw the killing with my own eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Avdi Banush was killed right in front of you. Why is it the case that you had never mentioned this before, and it's been ten years since the event. Why should you state this for the first time now? You didn't say this in your original statement nor in 2008.

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, Avdi Berisha. Banush is his father's name, but his full name is Avdi Berisha. Banush is the father. So I misspoke earlier. It is Avdi Berisha, and this is in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now the matter is quite clear, because your answer could lead us to conclude that Brajovic and Obrnovic who patrolled along the asphalt road killed the men that I heard of for the first time today. Now there is no more dilemma. You said that he was killed by sniper fire while he was standing 3 metres away from you. I will not be inquiring about this any further. Let us go back to Obrnovic who was patrolling the road through your village. Did he come to the centre of the village when the 14th of May events took place which you describe as the massacre in Cuska?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He was -- he just remained on the asphalt road, and then after they finished with Qyshk, they went to Pavlan and Zahaq.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mijo Brajovic is from Zahaq. This village does not have any boundary in the direction of your village, not for any practical intents and purposes?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Qyshk, Pavlan, and Zahaq are adjacent, but Qyshk is between Pavlan and Zahaq.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction. may I --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: What's the distance between Cuska and Zahaq?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are about 3 and a half kilometres or 4 kilometres between Qyshk and Zahaq.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter would like to correct a previous statement. The witness said "Qyshk is between Pavlan and Zahaq," and not as I stated earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Interpreter. Yes, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I just have to check this. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Save for the Brajovic family, how many more Serbian families were there in Zahaq?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were many. However, I did not have any contact with them personally, but there were many.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Are there any Serb families in Zahaq today? Do you have any knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everybody who has steeped their hands in the blood of Albanians does not live there any more. The people who did not commit any crimes, they still live there. They did not leave. Even during the war they didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how many Serb families stayed behind in Zahaq? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: About four or five households. Twenty families altogether, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: What can you tell us of the three Jasovic families from the village of Cuska? What happened to them? What became of them?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did what they did to Albanians, all those evil things, so they do not feel like coming back in Qyshk.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: According to your evidence so far, your neighbours Hashi [phoen] Perovic, Perovic's testimony, I could only gather that you lived next to the Jasovic family on friendly terms and amicably. This is the first time I hear something of the source. Can you tell us what are these horrid things that the Jasovic families did to you which would make them feel like not going back to your village?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zoran, Golub, and Vidoje, when the massacre happened, were together with the people who committed the massacre. I don't know whether they took part in the massacre or not. And I would like to say here that although all that massacre happened in the village Qyshk, no Serb suffered anything from the Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 36 of your statement you say that you had heard of the Vlahovic's visit from the refugees who came to the village on the 13th of May. You also say that the families came from different parts of Kosovo. What was the basis of knowledge of these refugees who came from different parts of Kosovo concerning this individual Vlahovic? How would they come to know who he was?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: People from Katundi i Ri, Cuf Tafilaj, for example, knew Vlahovic personally, and they had been told that all the refugees, all your guests should go to Qyshk because from there they will be sent to Albania, and on the 14th, all those people were in Qyshk.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In other words, the person who told you that this was what Vlahovic said was Cuf Tufilaj.

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was the same person that was beaten black and blue in the market in Peja that I mentioned earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Salipur.

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In whose' house was Cuf Tafilaj staying as a refugee?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Cuf Tafilaj was from Katundi i Ri, and he was not a refugee. The refugees that were staying in Katundi i Ri were told to go to Qyshk, and they came.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: That's why I'm asking you this. In paragraph 36, you say - since your sight is poorer I will read it out to you: "About the visit of Vlahovic in Katundi i Ri I learned from refugees who came to Cuska on the 13th of May, 1999, in the evening, and I remembered that they -- that they arrived around 70 to 80 people with their families from different parts of Kosovo." In other words, this was a refugee who told you this. When I asked you who this refugee was you tell me it was Chatunda [phoen] from Katundi i Ri. Now you tell me that he was not a refugee after all. Then please explain to me what is it that you stated in paragraph 36 and when did you mean when you say that you learned about the visit by Vlahovic from refugees? Who were the refugees you learnt this from?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true that I heard from the refugees Cuf was the one who had told them to go to Qyshk and escorted them. He escorted them up to Qyshk, and it is also true that I had contacts with the refugees. I asked them, What happened to you? and they told me that the police had ordered for them to go to Qyshk and then from there to Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: My question was: Which one of these refugees told you of Vlahovic's visit to Katundi i Ri? That's my question.

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Saban Shala from Graboc.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: What's the distance between Graboc and Cuska and Pec?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Gorazdac is about 2 kilometres away. It is 6 kilometres from us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Graboc is 6 kilometres away from Cuska?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Eight. It is a little further down than Lodja, about 6 kilometres I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And this individual knew Vlahovic, did he?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Cuf Tafilaj knew Vlahovic, Cuf Tafilaj from Katundi i Ri.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You will allow us then to draw our own conclusions from what you've just said. My next question: How many members of the Serbian forces did you know by sight, if not by name, and who were present in the village when the massacre took place? And I mean the village of Cuska?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew Rank Vlahovic and Obrnovic. They were the commander of the Klicina police station and of the Ozdren police station. I did not know the others, and as I said, they were masked.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Were there individuals among them who you found familiar but whose names you didn't know and whom you were able to recognise in the photographs you were shown subsequently? And who were present there on the 14th of May?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It is impossible -- it was impossible to recognise them because of their painted faces. As I said, only the whites of their eyes could be seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When did you have an opportunity for the first time after this event to sit down and talk to your neighbour Hazir Berisha?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you asking me before the war or after the war?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you about a brief period after the war and a short period before the end of the war. When was it for the first time after the 14th of May that you sat down and talked to your neighbour Hazir Berisha?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: When KFOR forces came to Kosova, the next day I went to Hazir Berisha. We had coffee together, and we discussed. Before that, it was very dangerous to go and visit people.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the neighbour tell you on that occasion that he had recognised certain individuals by sight but that he didn't know their names? And did you yourself, as I asked you today, see anyone whom you knew by sight but did not know their name?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nine members of my family had been executed and burnt, and we -- and I didn't think of discussing such things with him as you're putting to me now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You see, Mr. Kelmendi, what you've just mentioned now, justice for the victims is precisely the reason why I'm asking you this. It would be only natural that both you and Hazir wanted that those who were perpetrators of these crimes to be punished. That is precisely why I'm putting this question to you. It is not my intention to pry into your private matters. I'm only putting a natural question to you as to who you discussed who the potential perpetrators were with your neighbour. I just wanted to know whether there were any such discussions between the two of you.

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never discussed these things with him. I went to see him, to express him my happiness that he was better and alive, and that was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kelmendi, am I right if I say that Bajram Gashi did not, in fact, say that all the villagers went to the centre of the village because they were convinced that the Serbs would ship them off to Albania?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was lying down behind Deme's house, he wanted to go towards the centre, and I beckoned to him. I waved to him to come towards me, because I feared that they would be killed. It was Bajram and his wife and two daughters. I told him to come towards me because I feared that they would be killed. And I saved their lives, as a matter of fact, Bajram's life and his wife's and his two daughters', because had they gone there, they would be dead like the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe that this is an appropriate moment for our technical break. Following the break, I would have some 15 minutes of my cross-examination, and then I would have no further questions for Mr. Kelmendi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. We will have our first break now and resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Before we are waiting for the witness, regarding the statement of Dr. Alonso from 2006, I already tendered English version, and I want to say that in e-court we now have the B/C/S version, and I want also tender for the record just that version. It's D118 to be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Mr. Djordjevic. The English translation may be uploaded into e-court and incorporated into Exhibit D118. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kelmendi, am I correct when I say that from the place where you were, you were not able to see directly the toilet where Qaush Lushi was killed. This is something you refer to in paragraphs 47, 48, 49, 50 and 51 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw the Kalashnikov with my own eyes when it killed him in the outhouse. That is very true.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Did you see the place where he was killed from the place where you were? Were you able to see this outhouse or were you only able to see the policeman who was firing in a certain direction from the Kalashnikov?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, because it was 70 metres from the place I was, and I could see everything very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me if I'm correct when I say that you are not a direct eyewitness of what you refer to in paragraph 52 when you say that you heard that Skender Kelmendi was asked to save the life of his son by giving his truck away?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was Skender's wife that told me about Skender's case. I saw Qaush with my own eyes, and after Qaush was executed -- Qaush was executed after he gave the money to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for this. In paragraph 57 you talk about people about whom you later found out that they survived, and you even saw some of them personally. Can you please tell me, on the 15th of May, 2009, did you provide any additional information to the Prosecutor? This was four or five days ago -- five days ago.

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean here or in Kosova?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Here, five days ago, on the 15th of May, 2009.

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stated the same thing here, same as I stated in Kosova. There are many things that I can talk about with reference to Katundi i Ri and other incidents, but I did give a short statement about things that happened on the 14th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I just wanted to ask you about things relating to the specific events that we're discussing here. The first time that you mentioned seeing your neighbour Hazir Berisha as he was coming out of the window of Skender Gashi's house, which was on fire, it was burning, and you saw that his back was on fire. It was in flames. This is what you told the Prosecutor. Am I correct in understanding that this is what you said, that the clothes on his back were on fire?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. His leg had been kind of cut off, broken.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I would like to have your comment. Do you know that your neighbour Hazir Berisha, in his statement, did not mention at all that the clothes on his back were burning? He just mentioned burns on his face and broken, wounded leg.

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The forces inside the house shot at him, but it was God's will that he survived to tell what happened there in our village.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm just trying to get you to explain. Hazir Berisha did not say that the clothes on his backs were burning. You said that, so I would like to know where this difference comes from. This is what I wanted to ask you.

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: When Hazir left through the window, there was flames on his body, and then he fell on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Where on his body?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The whole body, as if his whole body was poured with benzine, with gas.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me if you know about the killing of three Serbian children on the river Bistrica across from your village of Cuska and close to the Serbian village of Gorazdevac? Do you know about this event? After the war.

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to complete my cross-examination of this witness with this. And I would like to thank the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, allow me to say a word or two about these children that were killed. Please, I would like to say something, with your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The village of Gorazhdec, these children went fishing on the river of Bistrice. It was the Serbs who threw the bomb and blamed the Albanians for that. Albanians do not have the tradition of killing children. It was the Serbs themselves who staged this just to blame the Albanians. It was the coming of the NATO forces to Kosova that helped the Albanians survive. Had they not entered Kosova, not a single Albanian would have survived.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Djordjevic, that was some additional comment in response to a subject which you raised in your last question. Do you want to ask anything further about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one question. Is the witness aware that the children were killed not by bombs but they were killed by gunshot fire? And if he knows that the Serbs did it -- did this, I would be grateful if the witness would tell the Trial Chamber how does he know this, who does he know it from, and how he can say that. I didn't ask him who killed the children, if it was the Serbs or the Albanians. I just asked him if he knew that these children had been killed. These are very serious charges. And if he can testify about this event, I would just briefly like to know who he learned that from this was done by the Serbs, how he knows that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was cutting hay. I'm a farmer. I was there with my tractor. The Serbs had gone there previously and had planted dynamite or bombs there. I heard the sound of the explosion. The Italian KFOR came there. They saw me with my tractor, asked me what had happened. They went to the spot, and it turned out that these three Serb children were fishing in Srbica. It is true that three Serb children were killed there, but the truth is that they were killed there by a bomb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That's the extent of your knowledge of this matter, is it, Mr. Kelmendi?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you, Your Honour. I will not have any more questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That's what you know about the death of these three children, is it, Mr. Kelmendi?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was cutting grass, mowing in my meadow --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You've told us that. I just wanted to be sure that you've said what you wanted to say about it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have nothing to add, Your Honours. I just told you that these civilians were killed between Gorazhdec and Pavlan in the river of Bistrica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As they were trying to fish by using explosives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Behar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Mr. Kelmendi, I just have two brief areas that I just wanted to revisit and hopefully clarify with you. First I wanted to ask you a couple of questions about your testimony previously about the refugees from Katundi i Ri that my learned friend from the Defence was asking you about. I know that you explained previously that Mr. Vlahovic had told these refugees to go to Cuska because the next day the Serb police were coming and would send the villagers from Cuska to Albania. And you were asked by my learned friend from the Defence, "Who were the refugees who told you this?" And I just wanted to make sure I had your answer correct, and I'm not sure, maybe the transcript didn't capture all of it. Am I right then you mentioned one name Cuf Tafilaj? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Cuf Tafilaj was the person who accompanied these refugees to our village, but the visitor that had come from Katundi i Ri was killed in Qyshk the following day.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Okay. And what I'm wanting to ask you about is who told you, if you remember, that Mr. Vlahovic had told them to come to Cuska. Was that Cuf Tafilaj who told you that?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: And is this the same -- is this the same person who was beaten by Mr. Salipur on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Cuf is from Katundi i Ri, whereas Isuf was a visitor, a guest stating in Katundi i Ri who was killed in Qyshk a day afterwards. Isuf is from Graboc village.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Okay. So what I'm trying to understand then in -- or to help the Court understand, are they two different people then, the person who you spoke to about what happened -- about what Mr. Vlahovic told him and the person in the market who was beaten by Mr. Salipur? Those are two different people?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Isuf is from Graboc whereas Cuf is from Katundi i Ri village.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Thank you. I think that, hopefully, is clearer for us. I notice, also, and I'm just looking at the transcript from when my learned friend from the Defence was questioning you. This is at page 25, line 20. The way it's recorded here, the question was -- he asked you: "My question was: Which one of these refugees told you of Vlahovic's visit to Katundi i Ri? That's my question." And the answer says: "Saban Shala from Graboc." Is that -- can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Saban survived, whereas Isuf was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Okay. I think that's hopefully somewhat clearer. Let -- let me ask you about a different area of questioning. You were asked today about how you knew that Mr. Brahovic was sent by Mr. Obrnovic, and I know yesterday - and I can just give the reference to the Court, this is at page 4719, line 23 - yesterday I asked you: "Did Mr. Brahovic tell you himself that Mr. Obrnovic had sent him?" And you answered: "Yes." And you were asked today by my learned friend from the Defence how you knew -- again, how you knew Mr. Brahovic was sent by Obrnovic. And you answered that well of course he had sent him. You explained why that made sense, but I wanted to be clear. Can you tell us, did Mr. Brahovic tell you that Mr. Obrnovic had sent you or is this something that you inferred?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Brahovic sent this person from Zahaq whose name I cannot recall right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Maybe I'll just ask that again; I'm not sure if we got the answer correctly. Did Mr. Brahovic tell you that Mr. Obrnovic had sent him?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. With a message that we should be calm and not afraid, that nothing was going to happen to us, that we would all be together at one place, and that nobody would touch us. This is what Mija said to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, sir. Those are my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Kelmendi, you'll be pleased to know that that completes the questions for you. The Chamber wishes to thank you for coming to The Hague and for the assistance that you've been able to give. The Chamber now wishes you well on your journey home, and the court officer will show you where to go. Thank you indeed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would also like to extend my gratitude to you, Your Honours. May I do that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours, very, very much. Now I'm freed, and I am sure that there is justice for all the peoples in the world. I am relieved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Gopalan.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. The next witness is Mr. Xhafer Beqiraj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Would you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- please read aloud the affirmation on the card that is shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Gopalan has some questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Beqiraj.

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Please could you state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ
utterances.text: Xhafer Beqiraj.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Mr. Beqiraj, where were you born?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ
utterances.text: I was born in the village of Kosave, Dragash municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And what is your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ
utterances.text: I was born on the 28th of April, 1970.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Where do you live now, sir?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ
utterances.text: I live in Prizren, but I'm temporarily residing in Vienna, Austria.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And what are you doing in Vienna, Austria?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ
utterances.text: I'm studying.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And what is it you're studying there?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ
utterances.text: Linguistics.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, did you testify in the trial of Slobodan Milosevic in this Tribunal in April 2002? If you could just --

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And have you recently had the opportunity to review your testimony in this case?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ
utterances.text: Yes. Yesterday I had that opportunity. However, I never had with me the testimony that I gave in the Milosevic trial. It was only yesterday that I had a chance to see it and review it.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And having reviewed this testimony yesterday, if you were asked the same questions today, would you provide substantially the same answers? Would your answers be the same?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I seek to tender the witness's testimony in the Milosevic case, that's 05122.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And that, Your Honours, will be assigned P00805.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Sir, do you recall giving a statement to the ICTY in October 2001?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Have you had the opportunity to review the statement recently? Thank you. [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And having reviewed the statement, I understand that you wish to make a correction to the statement. If I could call up 65 ter 05121, please, and I will take you to the correction -- the paragraphs in which you wish to make the correction.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: If we could go to page 5 of the English. That's the third paragraph from the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: While the statement is being called up on the screen, perhaps I could just read out the paragraph to you, and you could let us know the correction that you wish to make to the statement. You say: "Whilst waiting to cross, I also saw three girls, pretty girls, taken out of the line by the police with paramilitaries there as well. One was taken into the house nearby." What was the correction you wish to make?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ
utterances.text: These are two separate incidents. I saw two girls being separated from the line, taken in the direction of the forest. The convoy that was on foot asked for water. I was in the end of the tractor covered with blankets because it was cold and we didn't want to be noticed by the police. The person I gave water to said to me, See, these two girls are being taken towards the bushes. And this is what I saw. And later he said to me that another girl, a third girl, was taken away from the convoy to a house or a building nearby.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Beqiraj. And having made this correction, and this is to the third paragraph from the bottom of the page of the English, are you satisfied that this statement is true and accurate to your best -- the best of your knowledge and belief?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ
utterances.text: Yes, to the best of my knowledge and belief. Ten year have passed since. Therefore, this is to the best of my knowledge and belief.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I seek to tender 65 ter 05121.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: I'll now read out --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be assigned P00806, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: I'll now read out a brief summary of the witness's evidence. The witness is a Muslim male who lived in Prizren with his wife and two children in 1999. He will state that on the 28th of March, 1999, near the outskirts of Prizren, he saw a continuous column of people, including the old and sick, walking south from the direction of Djakovica. On that day, the police came to the house he was staying at in Prizren with his family. There were also many others staying in the house. The police told the occupants of the house that they had five minutes to leave the house or that they would be shot. The witness and the group he was with were told by the police the direction in which they had to head, and he will say that their movement out of Prizren had been planned well. The witness and his family, along with others, were directed by the police and paramilitary lines out of Prizren towards Albania. There was also VJ present. The witness will state that they travelled for 12 hours to the Albanian border. Throughout their journey to the border, they faced insults from Serbian forces. At the Albanian border, the witness saw young men being separated and taken away from the columns of people there by the police. Also at the border, the witness and others were ordered to hand over identification papers and vehicle licence plates. The witness and his family then passed through Morina and Kukes before eventually going to Tirana. That's the end of the -- my summary.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Sir, now I have some questions for you about your statement. Let's begin with the first night of the NATO bombing. This is in paragraphs 4 and 5, page 2, of the English. You say that you were at home with eight refugees who had come from the village of Opterusa, Orahovac municipality, who told you they had left the village in August 1998 as the area had been attacked by police supported by the VJ. You also say that there were a large number of refugees in your neighbourhood and in the town. Sir, which neighbourhood in Prizren did you live in?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ
utterances.text: I was living in the village -- in the neighbourhood of Jeta e Re in Prizren.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now these large number of refugees that you speak about that were in your neighbourhood, do you know where they had come from?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ
utterances.text: In fact, the refugees were not staying in my neighbourhood, but they were staying at Rruga e Ulqinit. I had left my neighbourhood together with my family and other families in the neighbourhood, and we went to Lagja e Ulqinit neighbourhood. There we stayed for two days, and from there then we were expelled by the Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Mr. Beqiraj, let me just stop you there. Perhaps it will assist you if I gave you an Albanian copy of the statement so I may direct you to the specific paragraph in your statement that I am referring to.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: With Your Honours' leave, may I do that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: I believe this information is on page 2 of your statement, the second last paragraph where you say there were a large number of refugees, maybe 50 in my immediate neighbourhood. In fact, there were many in the town. Now, this large number of refugees who were in your neighbourhood, do you know where they had come from? Have you found the correct paragraph? It's on page 2 of your statement, and it's the second last paragraph. Perhaps I will just read out the paragraph to you. It says: "There were a large number of refugees, maybe 50 in my immediate neighbourhood ..." and this is around the time of the NATO bombing when it began. If you recall, this large number of refugees who were in your immediate neighbourhood, about 50 of them, do you know where they had come from?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. They came from the surrounding areas of Prizren where fighting was going on and where there had been massacres and violations of all kinds. They had come from the villages of Krusha, Landovica, Pirane, and other surrounding villages. They had heard that horrible things had been happening, that young people were being ill-treated and separated from their families. So these young men had jumped from the tractors and come to our neighbourhoods or, rather, to Lagja e Ulqinit neighbourhood, and those people told us.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you also say that there were large number of refugees in the town. Which town is it that you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ
utterances.text: Prizren, Ulqini neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And just going back to your answer on the refugees that had left due to massacres and violations of all kinds, the ones that you say came from Krusa, Landovica, Pirane, and other surrounding villages. Do you know who was responsible for these massacres and violations?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ
utterances.text: On the basis of the stories that the people told me and their state of mind, I could tell that these massacres and all the events had been caused by the Serb forces. There had been horrible killings going on.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Did you speak to any of these refugees personally to obtain this information?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ
utterances.text: Yes. We were staying in one room, the males; and the women and the children were in another room so that they wouldn't hear the horrible stories. So within -- between us men, we discussed what had happened, why they had come there, and the owner of the house offered them shelter --

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ
utterances.text: -- to these young men.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: I now take you to another part of your statement and the English is paragraph 6 of page 2, and in the Albanian it's the last paragraph of page 2 and the first paragraph of page 3. There you say that "When the NATO bombing stopped, we could hear the local police shooting in the air with their machine-guns." Now, who are you referring to when you say the "local police"?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ
utterances.text: When I say "local police", I mean all the policemen that came from that area. They were in uniform, the regular police, but also civilian -- Serb civilians that had been given uniforms and had been armed by Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you know why these individuals were shooting in the air with their machine-guns?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ
utterances.text: Their aim was to create panic, to terrify people, and to tell them that something horrible was going to happen in the future, and that's what we believed, that something horrible would happen, because such things had already happened elsewhere, and you know about those.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, moving on to the day after the first NATO air-strikes. This is the 25th of March, and you say that on this day you decided to take your family to a safer place. So your uncle took them to your nephew's house in the town of Prizren. In the English this is para 7 of page 2. Now, sir, why was it that Prizren town centre was considered to be safer than your neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ
