utterances.text: The situation was alarming. Things were happening each and -- with each and every passing moment. There was danger at every corner. There were gunshots. So seeing the situation that the Serb forces were stationed at Progres Factory and there were Serb forces in the street armed and so on - and that factory was about 400 metres as the crow flies from us - we decided to send the women and children to the centre of the town because we knew that people from different nationalities lived there, and we thought it would be safer. And this is not something that only my family did. There were other families who had left earlier, before the 24th when NATO bombing started. Maybe only four or five families altogether remained in the family -- in the neighbourhood. The neighbourhood had been emptied of its inhabitants more or less.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And when you say that there were Serb forces stationed at the Progres factory, are you able to identify which forces were stationed at the factory, if you know?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I remember, but I think this is true. The police forces were stationed there together with different special units of the police. They had blue vehicles, and they would go back and forth towards the town, the centre of the town, and then back to the factory. That was -- that severed as a kind of a bases for them, this factory that I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, moving on to the 27th of March, by this stage your family had returned back to your neighbourhood, and you say that on that day at around 1900 hours, two Albanian neighbours of yours came to your house and advised your family that it would be safer for all of you to leave. Why -- let me just finish my question. Why would it have been safer for you to leave? What did they mean when they said that it would be safer for you to leave with your family?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ
utterances.text: As I said earlier, there were only about four families that remained in the neighbourhood, and the attacks were increasing. The gunshots were increasing. And keeping in mind the fact that -- that there was nobody else in the neighbourhood, we didn't know whether we were the wise ones to remain there or the other ones had been clever to leave. So we decided that all of us should leave and go towards the centre because it was safer there.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And that's what you say in paragraph 4, page 3, of your statement in English. You say: "It was our intention to go to the town centre in Prizren." And you go on to say that: "At that time we were still walking to town using the side roads to avoid the police." Why were you avoiding the police by using these side roads?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ
utterances.text: Prizren was full of policemen. They were everywhere. Paramilitaries as well were everywhere, and their presence was a threatening presence; it meant death to us. Other people had suffered before, so we didn't want to meet them or encounter them, and we went towards the centre by using side roads. That was the reason, because there were check-points and the police were patrolling the streets. So we wanted to avoid them as much as possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And when you say Prizren was full of policemen, do you recall what uniforms these policemen were wearing?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ
utterances.text: They circulated all over the town. They had blue uniforms, camouflage blue, as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And how about these paramilitaries who you say were everywhere? What were they wearing? If you recall.

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ
utterances.text: To my recollection, they were wearing green uniforms and green camouflage uniforms. These people were older, over 40 years old, that told me that they were not regular soldiers and that they were even more dangerous than the regular army because they could commit crimes with impunity. They also travelled and drove cars that they had painted in different colours and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now let's move on to the events on the morning of the 28th. This is when you went to a house in the outskirts of Prizren on Ulqini Street where you say there was a continuous column of people walking from the direction of Djakove. Some sick old people come injured, and they seemed very tired and exhausted. This is in the English, page 3, para 6. Now, this column of people you referred to, did you see them yourself?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ
utterances.text: I did not see this column of people with my own eyes, but I was told by other people. At one point, I was going to my house to get some papers. I then met some people who told me that it was dangerous to go there. Some of these people were from the convoy, from the column, and the convoy was endless. You could not see the end of it. People from all ages, infirm, elderly, people who were travelling in all kinds of vehicles to go towards Albania in order to be safe.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. These people who you met who were from the convoy, did they say where they had come from when you spoke to them?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ
utterances.text: I did not speak to them, but some people I knew that were from my neighbourhood told me that it was dangerous. I, in fact, was trying to cross the column, to pass there, but I was trying to find a moment to pass so that not -- so as not to be seen by the forces. The -- those people that I mentioned earlier that had left the column and came to the house where I was, they told us horrible stories. They told us how many people there were, that their numbers were increasing with every passing moment, and there were horrible stories that they had to tell. The street was full of the inhabitants of the area but also full of people that had come from the villages where these events had happened. It was an alarming situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, let's move on to events later in the day. This is in the English page 3, the last paragraph. You say: "At 1700 hours, police knocked on the door of the house we were staying at. They were in regular uniform with automatic weapons ..." What do you mean when you say "regular uniform"?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ
utterances.text: These were police uniforms. We called them regular uniforms. And the police had surrounded the neighbourhood from all sides and had given orders. Earlier, there had been gunshots from various types of guns, handguns and larger guns. This was preparation for expulsion. And then we heard the knock on the door. The owner of the house went out and spoke to them. We were staying close to where they were talking. The police gave him the order to leave the house in five minutes and go towards Albania because otherwise the worst would happen to us. This was the ultimatum that was given to everybody in that house but also other houses in the neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, did you see who it was that the owner of the house spoke to? You said that the owner of the house went out and spoke to them. Did you see who he spoke to?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ
utterances.text: I know that they were police forces and he was speaking to them. There was a corridor where I was staying. The door was to the left. And when the door opened, I only saw the arm of a policeman, and I could see the blue camouflage uniform. Then he came in. The owner of the house came in, and he said that the police gave me the order to leave the house in five minutes and go towards the border with Albania. We had to get out to the street in five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And you say in your statement, this is at page 4, paragraph one that: "After the ultimatum was given, we all decided to leave with our suitcases and other belongings. Once outside, everyone was throwing their personal effects onto the tractor trailer." Now, when you say "we all decided to leave with our suitcases," who were you with at this stage?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ
utterances.text: I was there with my family and other refugees. There were about 30 of us on the tractor trailer.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. You then say, this is on page 4, paragraph two: "We left the courtyard. We were sitting on the trailer. We had to travel between two lines of policemen, many of them. They told us which way to go before we left the neighbourhood. This had been planned very well." First when you say you had to travel between two lines of policemen, how did you know that these men were policemen?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ
utterances.text: I could tell by their uniforms that they were wearing. This was not the first time that I had seen these forces and these uniforms. They had committed massacres and had caused tragedies in other parts of the country that I had seen on television.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And these men that you saw, what uniforms were they wearing, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ
utterances.text: To my recollection, they had blue uniforms, blue camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And you also say that this had been planned very well. What do you mean when you say that this had been planned very well?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ
utterances.text: I have to say that this planning had not started on the day this happened. It had been prepared beforehand. That was the day when they implemented the plan for the expulsion of the population. I say that because the neighbourhood was surrounded in a very organised manner, and they directed us where we had to go, and the direction was only dictated by them. We couldn't go where we pleased.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And you say that there were many of them. Now, if you recall, how many were directing you out of your neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ
utterances.text: There was a large number of policemen; however, I cannot give you the exact number. I can only say that it was a very large number. The situation was such that I could not just sit there and count how many there were. We were trying not to be obvious and save our lives, but they were obvious everywhere. You could see them.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. You also referred to some other forces being present. This is in paragraph 3 and 4 of page 4 of the English, that there were police special forces who were also there. Did they say anything to you or the group you were with as you were heading out of your neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ
utterances.text: Yes. There were insults hurled at us of all sorts. They were also saying, "Where is KLA? Why are -- are they not protecting you? Where it Thaqi? This is not your country." And they were waving good-bye to us, some of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And in which direction were you directed by these forces?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ
utterances.text: The forces directed us towards Albania, around the town towards the Printex Progres industrial area and then towards Zhur.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. You also say that as you walked -- and I'm quoting: "As we would walked, the police and paramilitary lines were very tight. There was a VJ presence with soldiers and equipment, mortars, APC and other vehicles." Now, how do you know that there were soldiers present?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ
utterances.text: Where do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: In your statement you say -- this is in the English, page 4, para 7, and in the Albanian it's page 5, the second last paragraph. You say that when you were being led out of your neighbourhood the police and paramilitary lines were very tight. There was a VJ presence with soldiers.

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ
utterances.text: Yes. On one side there were policemen; on the other side we could see various kinds of green uniforms. Some of them had green masks on their faces in the form of nets, bandannas on their heads, and as I said, they were older than normal soldiers. That led us to believe that these were not regular soldiers but paramilitaries.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And how about the regular soldiers? Were there regular soldiers present there in addition to these paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ
utterances.text: The regular soldiers were constantly moving about in the vicinity of Printex and Progres industrial area. It was constantly on the move, but there where we were, there were police forces and paramilitary forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And these regular soldiers that were constantly moving that you just mentioned, did you see them yourself? And how --

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: -- did you know they were soldiers?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ
utterances.text: There were green tanks and armoured vehicles, and this led us to believe that those were soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. If you recall --

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ
utterances.text: Also, in Progres factory area there were different types of vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. If you recall, what were these soldiers wearing?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ
utterances.text: The soldiers wore green uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: I'd like to call up Exhibit P318, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And while we're waiting for the exhibit to come up, sir, you referred to different types of vehicles that you saw in the Progres factory area. I'm going to show you a number of photographs of vehicles. If you could let us know if you recognise any of these photographs as the ones you -- any of these photographs as representing the vehicles that you saw in the area on that day. We're now on page 1.

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ
utterances.text: To my recollection, the vehicle shown on photograph 2; on photograph 1, however, I'm not quite sure. I know that they were green, but there were different types of military vehicles in the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Could we move to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Did you see any of these vehicles there on that day?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ
utterances.text: Yes. The vehicle depicted on photograph number 7, then the one photograph number 6. I'm not quite sure about number 8, but there were also similar vehicles to this one there.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And if we could just move on to the final page of this exhibit. Did you see any of these vehicles?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ
utterances.text: I don't remember seeing these type of vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in your statement, as you were leaving Prizren you say you were "prevented from taking other streets than the ones where they wanted us to go to. We had an escort until we got out of town." Now, how is it you were prevented from taking other streets?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ
utterances.text: At every entry to the town there were Pinzgauers or smaller vehicles placed on the main roads, and there there would be policemen who were directing the crowd. This is how it was up to the exit from Prizren. Every road leading to the centre of the town was blocked by this type of vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And you say you had an escort until you got out of town. Who was it that escorted you out of town?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ
utterances.text: To my recollection, it was a green vehicle leading in front, leading the crowd.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Do you recall this vehicle from the set of photographs I just showed to you? Would you like to see them again? This green vehicle that you referred to leading you out of town.

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ
utterances.text: Yes, if you could show me the photographs again, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Could I call up P318, please. It's -- I'm sorry, it's still on the screen? No.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Are any of the vehicles on this first page the ones you -- the one you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Can we move on to the next page?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ
utterances.text: Yes. The photograph number 7 depicts the vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, you say that it took you and the group you were with 12 hours to reach the Albanian border. How far is Prizren from the Albanian border, if you know?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ
utterances.text: I would say 15 or 20 kilometres far from Prizren. I'm not maybe very accurate with the distance, but roughly that's what it should be.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And prior to this day, had you travelled to the Albanian border before?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ
utterances.text: No, never. I went up to the village of Zhur because had I travelled straight to the border, there I would have been subjected to many check-points. That's why I didn't see it reasonable to go towards that direction. As it was a border area, a border zone, there were more frequent checks in that area even before.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Now, you say that after Zur, this is paragraph 1, page 5 of the English, you say that: "On the way to the border after Zhur, we were constantly insulted by Special Police forces, same Special Police forces as the ones in town." What did these forces say to you?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ
utterances.text: These forces were using offensive language towards us. They were cursing. I would not be able to repeat here all the swear words they used. They would make gestures suggesting that they were going to slaughter us. They would say, "Where is the KLA to defend you? Where is Thaqi?" All these different types of threats and offensive language.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, I understand that you were travelling in a convoy. If you know, how big was this convoy?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ
utterances.text: You couldn't see the end of it. That's how long it was. It seemed endless. Even after we crossed into Albania, convoys continued to arrive at Kukes. Kukes was full of refugees who told their stories about what they had been through. Their state of mind showed how they terrify -- how terrified they were as a consequence of what had happened at the time. Kukes could not handle all these refugees, because the convoys were endless, crossing into Kukes for days in a row, for months in a row.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, the immediate group you were travelling, how many of you were there? Sorry, the immediate group you were travelling with. Do you know how many of you were together?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ
utterances.text: About 30, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, just moving on to the events at the Albanian border. You say your tractor was stopped at the Albanian border. This is paragraph 2 of page 5. Could you tell us who stopped the tractor you were in.

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ
utterances.text: When we approached the the customs office at the now Kosova-Albania border, and at the time, former Yugoslavia-Albanian border, there were two policemen one on one side and one on the other side. One of them was wearing a blue uniform. He resembled a customs police officer. They asked for all our identification papers and the licence plates. Some of the people didn't have the documents, and they were worried about what was going to happen to them. One of us knew how to speak Serbian better, and we decided that he handed over the documents. There next to us was an a huge pile of documents and registration plates.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. As I understand it, you were travelling as a part of a larger convoy. Did you see what happened to the identification papers or the licence plates of others who were in the convoy with you?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ
utterances.text: They suffered the same fate. For some it was easier; for some it was more difficult. For me it was easier because, as I've already mentioned in the first trial that I attended, myself and my family didn't get the worst of it. We were terrified. We were expelled from our own homes. We were denied the right to live in our own homes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ
utterances.text: Everyone was subjected to the same procedure.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And specifically, I'd asked you about what happened to the identification papers or licence plates of the others who were in the convoy with you on that day, if you saw.

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ
utterances.text: Yes, I did see it. The papers were collected, thrown on this pile. This pile was huge, pile of documents and other personal papers, registration plates, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And now I'd like to move on to some of the locations that you went to when you travelled from Prizren to your eventual destination. If we could call up 65 ter 615 and go to page 26, please. In your statement, you say - this is page 5, second last paragraph - while we wait for the exhibit to be called up. "So after the incident at the Albanian border, we then proceeded to the Albanian border. We arrived at Morina. We put some fuel in the tractor and proceeded to Kukes, arriving at 0700 hours the next morning. I think it was the 29th. I'm not 100 per cent sure. We left our tractor with one of our relatives, and we took a bus to Tirana."

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: If we could just zoom in on the top half of the page, please. Thank you. With the Court's usher, I would like the witness to mark some of the locations that he mentions in his statement. Is it possible to zoom in even further to the top-left half of the page? If we could just move the page up a little bit, please. Is it possible to move the page up? Sorry, the opposite direction. Yes. Thank you. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Sir, in your statement you mentioned Zur, and you say it was after Zur that your group was constantly insulted by the Special Police forces. Are you able to see Zur on this map? If you could circle Zur and mark it with an A.

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Next you say that you arrived at the Albanian border and that this is where you were ordered to surrender your ID and registration plates of the vehicles. Are you able to identify where this happened? If you could just place a circle around the approximate location where your IDs were taken away.

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: You have circled Morina.

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ
utterances.text: Morina, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And that was where your identification cards and licence plates were taken away?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's where the border is also, the border between Kosovo and Albanian.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And finally, before we move on, could you please morning Morina with a B, please.

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And then you say that you went to Kukes. If you could mark Kukes with a C.

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: I would like to tender this exhibit into evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be assigned P00807, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Sir, you say that you then went to Tirana with your family on that day, and you say that you then returned to Prizren on the 19th of June, 1999. This is in the last paragraph of the English. Why did you not return to Prizren with your family? Why did you return alone?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ
utterances.text: The situation was still unclear, uncertain, at the time. There were rumours that Kosova was free, that the NATO forces had entered it, but I didn't feel safe to take my family with me because of the mined areas, the booby-traps, and so on. That's why I decided to go on my own to check on the house to see what happened there. There were some minor damages to my house, but it was standing, it was in living condition, and I went back to collect my family and return to Kosova together with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And where was your family at this stage?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ
utterances.text: In Tirana.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And where were you and your family living in in Tirana?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ
utterances.text: We lived in tents.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have one final topic that would take me approximately ten minutes. I'm happy to begin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will have the second break now, and you can conclude after that. We will resume at 5 minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Gopalan.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Sir, I have a few questions for you on my final topic today. That's on the education system in Kosovo in the 1990s. I'd like to take you back to the beginning of your statement. In the English this is paragraph 3, page 2, and there you say that before the war you were a schoolteacher of Albanian language in a primary school. And you also say that the Serbian policy on education was a discriminatory one and that the schools were for the benefit of the Serbs, not the Albanians. Could you explain for us what you mean when you say the Serbian policy on education was a discriminatory one?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ
utterances.text: Bearing in mind that from 1989 a policy was pursued that divested Albanians of all their rights, also including their autonomy. In 1990 they started to commit some poisonous acts in the schools whose perpetrators were never found. They remained a mystery. Even today some inquiries have been conducted and nothing has been discovered. Serb perpetrators committed them with the intention of having only a Serbian curricula in the school. Albanians didn't agree with that. Therefore, they set up their parallel system of education. After experiencing what I mentioned in the high schools, then in 1992, if I'm not mistaken, all Albanian students and high -- and high school students were deprived of their right to be educated in the same facilities that they had been going on until then. It became forbidden for them to enter the university premises and the high schools, whereas the primary schools continued to function in two shifts. The Serbs went to school in the morning together with some other ethnicities, and the Albanians in the afternoon with a shortened programme.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Sir, let me just stop you there to clarify some things that you have just said. You say, "After experiencing what I mentioned in the high schools." What is it that you experienced in high school as a high school student if that's what you mean. You were referring to the parallel system of education when you said that.

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ
utterances.text: The parallel system started later, after the Albanians were deprived of their right to education. In this situation, they came up with a parallel plan of education whereby the high -- and higher school students started to go to private facilities. They were schools turned into -- houses turned into schools, that is, make-shift schools.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And as a schoolteacher, did you have experience of this discriminatory policy in education that you referred to?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ
utterances.text: Yes. Not only myself but all my generation of teachers and of students were subjected to this discrimination, which is a fact of life now because much has been spoken about that and efforts have been made to find a solution to this issue until 1970.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me stop you there. As a schoolteacher, when you were teaching in this primary school, are you able to give us any specifics examples of discriminatory practices that you experienced?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ
utterances.text: Yes. In the school where I -- school where I used to teach - it was called Emin Duraku school until 1991. The Serb regime removed the plaque that was in front of the school which bore the Albanian -- an Albanian name and put the name of a Serb personality instead. That was the first step towards discrimination. Then, in light of the fact that the Serbs and other ethnicities worked from 7.00 to 2.00, 1400 hours, with a very small number of students - which was about 470, if I'm not mistaken - the Albanians who worked from 1500 to 1900 had to teach about 1.200 students. We didn't have the right -- didn't have access to all didactic means to educate our -- teach our students. We were forced to work in extraordinary circumstances, and that was for us a total discrimination. This was the case in education and in all walks of life. That's why we came to the point where we came later.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And when you speak about not having access to all didactic means to teach students, are you able to provide any specific examples of what you're referring to when you say didactic means?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ
utterances.text: Yes. I mean the library, for example, I couldn't have access to it or other teaching materials. We didn't have access to the laboratories available in the schools because they were used only by the Serb students. We were obliged to work, all of us, in one common hall. It was a chaotic situation. We were reduced to a very limited space. But nevertheless we worked even under these circumstances in order to be able to provide some form of education to our students until 1992 when the teaching was completely interrupted.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And what time period is it that you're referring to when you say, for example, that there was no access to the library? You say that the teaching was interrupted in 1992, but how much before 1992 did you -- how much before 1992 was it that these examples that you give began, the lack of access to teaching materials and so forth?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ
utterances.text: I started to work in the Emin Duraku primary school in 1995. Until that time, I was a student, which means that I experienced this form of discrimination both as a student, being obliged to study under extraordinary conditions, but also as a teacher. The situation started prior to 1995, but I cannot give you an exact date now.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Before I finish off, I'd just like to take you to your statement again.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: If we could call up P00806, please. And if we could have the English and Albanian on the page. Let's start with page 1 of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Sir, in the Albanian statement on your screen, you will see that approximately halfway towards the bottom of the page there's a mention of two dates of interviews, one in April 1999 and another one in October 2001.

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And could we move on to the second page, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Could you read for us, please, the first paragraph of the page that is before you.

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ
utterances.text: "The investigators note: This statement includes and expands the 'unsigned' interview of this witness not read over by investigator Yves Roy on 14 of April, 1999, in Tirana, Albania. My name is Xhafer Beqiraj; I was born -- "

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Just the first paragraph. Now, what you have just read out, does that accord with your recollection that you gave an interview in 1999 that was not read back to you nor signed by you?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And when you gave this interview in Tirana, do you remember where you were?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ
utterances.text: I was at a hotel, but I don't recall the name of this hotel now.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. I have no further questions for you at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Beqiraj. My name is Dragoljub Djordjevic, and I am the Defence counsel for the accused. I will have several questions for you with a view to shedding light on some parts of your evidence before this Tribunal and parts of your statement that you gave to the OTP. I will take up from where my learned friend finished, and that's the statement that you gave on the 14th of April, 1999, in Albania, in a hotel, the name of which I cannot recall at present. You confirm that you gave the statement without having signed or read it. Tell me, you were present in Albania at the time as of which date prior to the 14th of April, 1999, when you gave the interview?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ
utterances.text: I was present in Albania from the 29th of March, 1999, where we -- when we were driven out by force.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Gopalan.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's not -- just to clarify, Defence counsel refers to the statement not being signed or having been read by the witness, but I believe the section read out by the witness refers to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Look, Ms. Gopalan, no need to worry about that sort of fine detail. We have read what is there and appreciate the circumstances. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Carry on, please, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can all the extra microphones please be switched off.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You told me that you left together with your family from Kukes to Tirana; is that right?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You came to Tirana on what day? Do you recall the date?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ
utterances.text: Yes. We stayed in Kukes only until the afternoon of the 29th of March, and that afternoon we set out for Tirana. We arrived in Tirana on the 30th of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Beqiraj, can you tell me who was present when you gave the statement on the 14th of April, 1999, in a hotel in Tirana? Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ
utterances.text: I remember an investigator and an Albanian interpreter whose names I can't recall now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: How did you come into contact with the OTP investigator, which led you to eventually giving a statement to him on the 14th of April that we've been referring to?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ
utterances.text: They came to the camp where we were accommodated in those tents I mentioned. Then an interpreter and the investigator asked us to give statements about what had happened, how -- how had it come that we had arrived in Tirana and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Was this the only statement you gave on that day, or did you give a statement to someone else as well?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ
utterances.text: I gave only the statement in Tirana. I didn't give any other.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Did you give any other statements subsequent to this one?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ
utterances.text: Yes, in Kosova, if I remember right, in 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: When you gave the statement in 2001 in Kosovo, was there mention of the 14th of April statement, the one that you gave on the 14th of April, 1999, in Tirana?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember if the same investigator who interviewed you in Tirana was there in -- in Kosovo as well?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ
utterances.text: I think no. It was another investigator.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Did this other investigator tell you before you gave the statement on the 6th of October, 2001, which you confirmed to my learned friend that you did give, that he had that other 1999 statement of yours, and did he ask you if you wanted to change or supplement anything that you had stated back in 1999?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: At the time, in October of 2001, did you have the occasion to read the 14th of April, 1999, statement in its entirety?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Your previous answer said that it was shown to you. Was it only shown to you as a piece of paper or were you shown its contents?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I have no recollection of it at all, because now ten years have passed and these are minor details which for me are difficult to recall. And after what we have been through, we all were under stress and wanted to do away, obliterate from our mind those events. To this day, many people in Kosova live under stress as a result of those events; and I suffered the same stress and trauma to this day, because to go through such a horrible situation, it's not easy for you to forget. Not only what I saw, but also what I saw through the media outlets, through the peoples -- people narratives. It was a question that did not relate to an individual but to an entire nation. It was kind of common suffering, I would say. So many things have slipped my memory after such a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Beqiraj, I understand you fully, and I sympathise with you. Unfortunately, this is a court of law where in addition to expressing sentiments and emotions we also need to concentrate on the facts. I do sympathise with your experience, but we nevertheless have to deal with facts. Therefore. I will proceed along that line.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we again call up -- or, we have it, rather, I think, the 6 October 2001 statement on our screen. I'm interested in the top of page 2 in both Albanian and English. The statement has already been admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Look at paragraph 1, investigators note which reads: "This statement includes and expands the 'unsigned/not read over' interview of this witness taken by investigator Yves Roy on the 14th of April, 1999, in Tirana, Albania." How are we to interpret this statement or the paragraph written by the investigator and signed by you? Tell us. We would really like to clarify what this is all about.

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ
utterances.text: I never had any problems with a court of law. This is my second time to be present in such a court of law. I have no legal experience. I was told to sign the statement, and I did sign it thinking that it was a matter of signing the statement that I just gave. So I have nothing else to say to your question. If I were a lawyer, I would be in a better position to know how to act. Being not a lawyer, I know no better.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Beqiraj, my question was not of legal nature. It relates to the facts. May I conclude, based on your answer, that you, in fact, never had an opportunity to familiarise yourself with the 14th of April, 1999, statement gave to Yves Roy --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Yes, to Yves Roy.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And that the other investigator, Clifford Smith who made this statement --

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ
utterances.text: Frankly speaking, I don't remember. Frankly speaking, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: That earlier statement, and you had never had an opportunity to read it. I can't believe that you wouldn't be able to recall ever reading a statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, the witness has told you he doesn't remember what you are asking about at the commencement of the second interview. At the end of the first statement, you will see a heavy note: "This statement was not re-read to the witness," and that, I would suggest to you, fully explains why at the commencement of the second there is the note by the investigator, not by the witness, that the first statement was unsigned and not read over.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: But at the beginning, "This statement includes and expands."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There can be no mystery about it. If you read the two statements, you will see that the first statement is there and there are additions. You are very familiar with that, and that's why the first statement is included. Perhaps I should become the witness, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it will be, after all, up to you to adjudicate this matter to the end. I wanted to draw your attention to the differences between the first and second statement, and I will not be able to put these questions now since evidently the witness has never read the first statement and cannot testify to the fact that whatever he said at the time was indeed recorded in the statement. I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That is not the view that I would understand of it, Mr. Djordjevic. He did not -- it was not read over to him when he made it in 1999. In 2001, a statement is made which includes what was said in 1999. Now, there must have been some revision of what was said in 1999 during the interview in 2001. What is of importance to this Chamber is whether in any material part of the 2001 statement there is some error, some oversight, or some omission. I would suggest you might concentrate on the content rather than the way it was prepared. It will be quicker, and it will be of more use to us. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will proceed that way. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You said that you were a teacher of the Albanian language immediately before the war, in a school called Emin Duraku. Tell me, were you a teacher within the regular Serbian school system of the Albanian language, or were you a teacher within the parallel Albanian schooling system existing at the time?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ
utterances.text: I said before, and I said when I gave the statement, that after the discrimination, after the dangers we were faced with as of 1990, we -- Albanian students as a result of the Serb discriminatory policy, the Albanians and the Serbs were separated in two different groups and shifts. The high schools and the universities were closed to Albanian students. This is a well-known fact. We have staged many protests against that situation, asking for the redressing of this right, asking for education for our students. Under that situation, we were obliged to set up the parallel system. This is what I explained earlier. Otherwise, hadn't we done this parallel student -- education, our students would have been deprived of any education at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You gave me an answer that is quite general, and these are matters that we heard from a number of witnesses testifying here. My question had to do specifically with the school you taught in, namely the Emin Duraku school. Can you tell me whether you continued teaching in the school throughout the period, or did you switch to teaching in different private homes under a schooling system organised by ethnic Albanians at the time?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ
utterances.text: I said earlier that during that decade I was both a student and a teacher, meaning that I experienced two things or the same situation as from two different angles. In 1992, we enrolled in this parallel education system, because -- THE INTERPRETERS: Correction.

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ
utterances.text: -- we wanted to enroll in the normal education system, but the police surrounded the premises and did not allow us to enter these premises. Then after some months being left without any schooling, we were obliged in 1992/1993, if I am not mistaken, in March, to start learning as students in private homes. The same was the case with the high school students who tried to find make-shift facilities to get their education. The primary schools continued to function in the same facilities that the Serb kids went. The situation in which we were obliged to work was a discriminatory one. Nobody can deny that, because there are facts to prove it. There are documents. It's a well-known fact for all.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Again, your answer was quite a general one. But you said that the elementary schools, including the Emin Duraku school, continued their activities and that students, including ethnic Albanian students, continued getting their education in these schools. Am I right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: As a teacher of the Albanian language, were you employed, you yourself?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ
utterances.text: Yes, from 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Who were you receiving your salary from as of 1995?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ
utterances.text: We received our salaries from the Albanian leadership at that time, because Albanians were segregated. They had their own programmes, their own contributions paid by the people in general to pay for the salaries of the teachers as much as they could afford to pay in order to provide education to the kids, to prevent them from remaining illiterate. There was a noble act, because the right to schooling was denied to the Albanian students. I said earlier that all the facilities were closed down. This made us -- this injustice, this discrimination, made us to switch to this form of education both for the primary, for the high schools, and also for the university.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Have you ever been employed within the Serbian and former Yugoslav state education systems?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ
utterances.text: No. But even those who were employed from 1990 were driven out of their jobs, were dismissed, and Kosova became a social case. The situation was deplorable. People were fired from their jobs and were unemployed. So poverty increased, discontent grew, because discrimination was widespread. It was not only in education but in all spheres of life.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: If things stood indeed the way you put them, how come you were allowed to use the public educational facilities of the Republic of Serbia for your educational purposes such as, for instance, the Emin Duraku primary school where you told us the Serb students were taught in the mornings and ethnic Albanians in the afternoons?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ
utterances.text: Firstly, these facilities did not belong to the Serb Republic, they belonged to Kosova where the overwhelming majority of the population are Albanians, about 92 per cent. Only 5 per cent were Serbs. The remainder were other ethnicities. This is not the place to discuss those issues, but the aid was provided for by the people who were in the better economic situation who had some private activities as well as by Albanians who worked abroad. They contributed to this system of education in Albanian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Am I right when I say that the authorities of the Republic of Serbia did not prevent your children from attending the Emin Duraku school, the 1.200 pupils you referred to?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ
utterances.text: I think I was quite explicit in my statement. I'm repeating it, that in the primary schools it was possible to continue education in the public facilities, but for the high schools and for the universities it was completely forbidden. You know very well that an effort was made through the Sant'Egidio Agreement for -- to resolve the question of the Albanian education, but it failed. So Albanians didn't get their rights to education.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the Sant'Egidio Agreement. Do you have knowledge to the effect that the Serbian authorities had deferred several university facilities to ethnic Albanians? Were you aware of that, and if so, which were these facilities that were handed over to the Albanians under the agreement? We're referring to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can Mr. Djordjevic repeat the year he mentioned.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- recollection. Maybe as a result of that agreement some facilities may have been handed over to fool the international public that Albanians were having access to their education. But I was a student myself at that time in Prishtina, and I studied in a private home. We used to sit on the floor without having any benches, any facilities. In this situation, the entire generation had to get education in such miserable conditions. And often we were subjected to police assaults, raids. They came and confiscated school materials and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was asked by the interpreter to repeat the year, and the year was 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: This is my final question in relation to the schooling system. Having been a student and having been involved in the Kosovo educational system, do you know or did you not know that certain university facilities were handed over to ethnic Albanians, Albanian professors and students? Do you know that they were handed over directly and given to them to use freely, and if so, do you know which ones?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ
utterances.text: I don't remember now because a long time has passed to tell you which facilities were handed over, but they were minor ones and very few in numbers and in not good conditions. They were simply handed over to Albanians to give the impression before the public, international public, that Albanians were being given such facilities. But most of them, most of these facilities, were not accessible to us. This is a fact. I don't know which specific facility may have been handed over.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I should like to stop my cross-examination of the witness until tomorrow because we are already one minute beyond our time for today, to work according to the changed schedule you informed us of. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Djordjevic. We need to adjourn today to continue tomorrow morning at 9.00. Mr. Beqiraj, an officer of the court will assist you with the directions, and we will look forward to hearing you again tomorrow morning. Could I say, Mr. Djordjevic, that we would appreciate if you could conclude your cross-examination in the first session, which will give you altogether about two hours of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: It will be for certain so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm just anxious that we finish the witnesses listed for this week this week. We adjourn now and resume tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 21st day of May, 2009, at 9.00 a.m. 17 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
